title: News of God's Grace: A Mountain Prayer Experience
author: Evangelist Allan Mukwasi
excerpt: On the 8th of December 2019, I was diagnosed with influenza...
content:
On December 10 at 5:47 PM, eight of us – Preacher Nobhula, Secretaries Mutonhore, Matienga, Madongorere, Jerera, Somerai, Dreamer Manyengavana, and myself – set out for Yanas Mountain in Ras Al Khaimah. Our journey was quiet, filled only with hymns. In spirit, we were already climbing, each note drawing us nearer to God's presence.

We arrived around 7:00 PM and, since we had no women or children with us, we climbed straight to the top. It took about 45 minutes. When we reached the summit, we began with humble confession. The Holy Spirit was present, and our Dreamers received visions and prophecy, each message guiding those present. As we worshipped, it felt as if heaven joined our chorus.

While we were still praying, the sound of cars approached the mountain base. Soon, over 30 vehicles had surrounded our parked car. I encouraged the brethren, "Let's sing louder so that those below know we are worshipping." The vehicles began circling the mountain, honking loudly. I decided to go down and meet them.

Halfway down, I met two Arab men in white garments. I called out "Mafi Mushkila" (No problem), but they kept their distance. When I reached the base, more than 25 men surrounded me. They spoke rapidly in Arabic, but I simply replied, "No Arabic, Mafi Mushkila. Only praying up there."

I told them, "My name is Allan Mukwasi. I am here with seven brethren in Christ. We are members of the African Apostolic Church under the divine leadership of Paul Mwazha of Africa. We came for special prayers, and these garments are our consecrated prayer attire."

The atmosphere changed to joy and laughter. One elder, Sunil, offered us a quieter place to pray and asked if we needed food or warmth. I explained we were fasting and had all we needed. Before parting, they asked us to pray for their community. I took Sunil's contact and apologised for any distress caused, assuring them we would seek permission in the future. They received this with goodwill.

I returned to the mountain top, and we continued in prayer with renewed unity and divine purpose. What began as tension ended in peace and fellowship. God turned a moment of misunderstanding into news of His grace, proving that fear yields to faith and strangers can become friends through His presence.

title: Mr Gambe - Overdue Pregnancy Testimony
author: The African Apostolic Church Publicity
excerpt: My wife was pregnant for two years and two months...
content:
My wife was pregnant for two years and two months but could not give birth. We spent a lot of money looking for help but found none. I then met members of the African Apostolic Church who advised that our problem could be solved there. I sent my wife to the church while I stayed behind. She later told me that church elders had prayed for her and that after three days she would be helped.

Indeed, after three days I was informed that she was well. I asked whether it was a boy or a girl, but I was told there was no baby — she had been carrying goblins for the past two years and two months. When I saw her, she looked like a young girl again. I immediately joined the church after that experience.

title: Mai Muvhangeri Musimwa - Infertility
author: The African Apostolic Church Publicity
excerpt: After years of infertility, a dream of Mutumwa Paul Mwazha...
content:
I was married in 2003 but could not conceive. I had a dream in which Mutumwa Paul Mwazha came to me, flying, and landed next to my bed. He told me to join the church and gave me directions to find it. I followed the instructions in the dream and went to the church, where I shared my dream and my problem with the elders.

They prayed for me the first time I came. On another day, I joined the queue for prayers, but the elders removed me from the line, took me aside, and prayed for me again. They told me, nokutenda uchabatsirwa (by faith you will be helped).

A month later, I became pregnant, and we named the child Nokutenda. Later, in January, my husband was struck by lightning. I prayed, and when he came home, his socks were burnt, but his feet were untouched. I thank God for the help I received through His messenger, Mutumwa Mwazha.

title: Anonymous Member - Vehicle Accident
author: The African Apostolic Church Publicity
excerpt: While repairing a lorry at work, the safety stands slipped...
content:
While repairing a lorry at work, the safety stands slipped, and the vehicle fell to the ground while I was still underneath. I do not know how I escaped, but I left all my tools under the vehicle. Although I felt pain and struggled to dress myself at first, I eventually recovered. What amazed me was that I had been told about this incident in church before it happened.

Lightning also struck at home when my mother was cooking. The cooking stick broke instantly, and my little sister was thrown into the fire, but she was unharmed. These experiences have shown me the power that abounds in VaPostori VeAfrica.

title: Beliefs and Practices of the African Apostolic Church
author: The African Apostolic Church
excerpt: The African Apostolic Church follows strict biblical teachings regarding food, alcohol, appearance, and worship, based primarily on the laws given in the first five books of the Bible.
content:
Food

In the African Apostolic Church, there are specific dietary requirements that differ from many other religions. These practices exist because the church follows the laws and statutes found in the first five books of the Bible given to Moses, rather than adopting reforms common in many modern denominations. The dietary rules are outlined in detail in Deuteronomy 14:1–21 and Leviticus 11:1–47. These passages define which foods are considered clean and acceptable for consumption and which foods should be avoided.

Alcohol

Members of the African Apostolic Church are prohibited from consuming alcohol. This teaching is based on the belief that God created the world good, as stated in Genesis 1, and therefore humans should not alter what God has made good. All human beings are created in the image of God and deserve dignity and respect. This belief is known as the sanctity of life. Consuming substances that dull the senses and potentially compromise personal dignity is therefore discouraged. Biblical teachings regarding this principle are further supported in 1 Corinthians 6:9–10 and Ephesians 5:18.

Yeast

The African Apostolic Church also discourages the consumption of yeast. This belief originates from an event recorded in The Divine Commission of Paul Mwazha of Africa, in which a divine message was received while bread was being eaten. Scientifically, during the bread-making process yeast, which is a fungus, ferments glucose and produces carbon dioxide and alcohol as byproducts. Because the alcohol produced during fermentation does not completely evaporate during baking, consuming yeast-based bread may involve consuming traces of alcohol. For this reason, yeast products are avoided.

Tattoos and Makeup

The African Apostolic Church discourages any form of bodily marking or alteration of one's natural appearance, including tattoos and excessive makeup. The belief is based on the understanding that human beings are created in God's image and that God's creation is perfect. In the Bible, tattoos and the act of cutting oneself are often associated with pagan or idol worship. During the time of the Israelites, followers of the idol Baal practiced rituals that involved cutting themselves as part of their worship. Judges 6:25 instructs believers to destroy such practices, stating: 'Tear down your father's altar to Baal and cut down the Asherah pole beside it.' Therefore, altering one's body in this way is viewed as participation in practices associated with idolatry.

Removing Shoes During Worship

During worship in the African Apostolic Church, members remove their shoes. This act symbolizes reverence and recognition of being in the presence of God. The practice is based on the account of Moses and the burning bush in Exodus 3:5, where God instructed Moses to remove his sandals because he was standing on holy ground. In the same spirit, members remove their shoes when worshipping to acknowledge the holiness of God's presence.

Men Lifting Hands During Prayer and Women's Modest Dressing

These beliefs are influenced strongly by 1 Timothy 2:8–13. Men are encouraged to lift their hands during prayer as a symbol of sincerity, purity, and submission to God, following the instruction to pray while 'lifting up holy hands without anger or disputing.'

Women are instructed to dress modestly, emphasizing that inner character is more important than outward appearance. This principle is also reflected in Isaiah 3:16. Women should avoid excessive adornment or clothing that encourages pride or the belief that one's value is determined by appearance. Instead, a person's worth should be reflected through their heart, humility, and good deeds.

Worship of Ancestors

The African Apostolic Church rejects the worship of ancestors. While respect for family heritage is acknowledged, elevating ancestors to the level of divine beings is considered unbiblical. Worship is reserved for God alone. Exodus 20:3 states clearly: 'You shall have no other gods before me.' Further warnings against idolatry are also found in Exodus 20:3–7 and 1 Corinthians 10:14–22.

Hair for Men and Head Covering for Women

Biblical teachings from Leviticus 19:27 and 1 Corinthians 11:2–16 influence beliefs regarding hair and head coverings. In this tradition, men are encouraged to keep their hair natural without elaborate styling, reflecting confidence in being created in the image of God. Scripture reminds believers that while humans often focus on outward appearance, God looks at the heart.

Women are encouraged to cover their heads as a sign of modesty and humility. While women may grow their hair long, it should be covered and not arranged in elaborate styles such as braids or twists that may draw excessive attention to outward appearance. The emphasis again remains on inner character rather than external display.

Church Attire

The clothing worn during worship is guided by teachings found in Ezekiel 44:17–20. Members typically wear white garments when attending church services. Men and women both wear white clothing, symbolizing purity and unity, while women also wear a white head covering and belt. This uniform style of dress represents spiritual preparation and respect, reflecting the belief that attending church is equivalent to entering the presence of God.
